opus-5.5.text:
I think anticipated regret is a useful signal, but a poor master. It's worth separating what the feeling is tracking from the feeling itself.

When people imagine spending fifteen years on a long-horizon project, say a career in academic philosophy, building an institution, or a slow-burn research agenda, and then transformative AI arrives in year six and makes it all moot, they feel a pang. Part of that pang is legitimate. It reflects a real change in expected value: if there's a substantial chance the world is radically transformed within a decade or two, then projects whose payoff is concentrated far in the future really are worth less in expectation. That isn't a psychological quirk. It's just discounting by the probability that the payoff never arrives, or arrives into a world where it no longer matters. So the first thing I'd say is: do that calculation honestly. Weight outcomes by how likely you are to reach them.

But regret adds something the expected-value calculation doesn't, and that's where I'd be more cautious. Regret is asymmetric in how we imagine it. We vividly picture the scenario where we bet on the long project and AI interrupted it. We much less vividly picture the scenario where we pivoted everything toward short timelines, the transformation came later or more gradually than expected, and we'd abandoned work that would have been enormously valuable. Both are regrettable outcomes. If you only rehearse one of them, your anticipated regret is biased, and you'll systematically overcorrect.

There's also a deeper point about what "interrupted" means. Many projects have value that isn't all back-loaded. A research career builds skills, relationships and judgement along the way, and those transfer. An institution can do good in year three even if it never reaches its year-twenty vision. So I'd encourage people to look at the shape of the value curve rather than just the endpoint. Projects that pay out continuously, or that build robust capacities, are much less exposed to interruption than projects that are all-or-nothing at the end.

And some of the most important work is valuable precisely in the worlds where things go well. If transformative AI goes badly, very little of anything we're doing will matter. If it goes well, there may be a long future in which the foundations we lay now, in ethics, in institutions, in our understanding of what we value, matter a great deal. So there's an argument that you shouldn't count the interruption scenario purely as a loss for long-term projects. In some of those worlds the project is cut short. In others it becomes more important.

So my practical advice would be roughly this. Take the shortened expected horizon seriously in your numbers. Favour, at the margin, projects that deliver value along the way or build transferable capacities. But don't let a one-sided sense of anticipated regret push you into treating the most dramatic timeline as certain. Try to choose the portfolio you'd be able to defend afterwards across the full range of ways the future could go. That's a better test than asking which single outcome you'd most hate to have missed.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that possible interruption lowers a long-horizon project’s expected value, but argues against letting anticipated regret drive an overcorrection: the project may still matter in futures where AI goes well, and its value may accrue along the way.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is a really interesting question, and it's one that I've been thinking about quite a bit, partly because it bears on my own life choices as well as on how we think about longer-term projects more generally.

So the basic worry is something like this. Suppose you're working on a project that might take ten or twenty years to pay off — a long research program, building up an institution, writing a big book, whatever it is. And suppose you also think there's some substantial chance that transformative AI arrives before that, and that when it arrives it either does the thing you were trying to do much faster and better than you could, or it changes the world so much that the project no longer matters in the way you'd hoped. Then there's a natural thought: "Well, if that happens, I'll regret having spent all those years on it." And the question is how much weight that anticipated regret should get.

My view is that anticipated regret is a useful signal, but it's a signal, not the thing itself. What it's often pointing at is a real feature of the decision — namely that the project's value is contingent on a particular future arriving, and you should be discounting for that. So if you think there's a fifty percent chance the project gets interrupted before it yields anything, then in a straightforward expected value sense, you really should be roughly halving the value you assign to it, and asking whether it still beats the alternatives. That's just correct, and the regret is a sort of emotional bookkeeping that reminds you to do that calculation.

But I think there are a couple of ways people go wrong with it. One is that they feel the regret much more vividly than they feel the symmetrical regret in the other direction. If you abandon a valuable long-term project because you expected AI to interrupt it, and then AI turns out to be slower than you thought, or turns out not to obviate the work, then you've also made a mistake — and often a costly one, because you've thrown away years of compounding progress. People tend to under-weight that scenario because it's less dramatic. So I'd want to insist on symmetry: anticipated regret cuts both ways.

The second thing is that regret is often tied to outcomes rather than decisions, and I think the right thing to evaluate is the decision. If you made a reasonable bet given what you knew, and it didn't pay off because the world went a different way, that's not really something to regret in the deep sense. You can feel disappointed, but you shouldn't feel that you did the wrong thing. And I think separating those two is important for being able to act under uncertainty at all. If you demand that every project be robust to every scenario, you end up doing nothing, or only doing very short-horizon things, and that's its own kind of failure.

There's a third consideration, which is that a lot of long-term projects have value along the way, not just at the end. If you're building up expertise, or relationships, or a community, or a body of ideas, a lot of that is useful even if the grand culmination never happens. And in a world where transformative AI does arrive, having people who've thought carefully about the relevant questions and have standing and credibility may actually matter more, not less. So I'd encourage people to look at the shape of the payoff curve rather than just treating it as all-or-nothing at the end.

And then the last thing I'd say is a bit more personal. I think there's a risk that the AI timelines discourse makes everything feel provisional, so that people are constantly hedging and never really committing to anything. I don't think that's a good way to live or a good way to do useful work. It's fine — sensible, even — to lean towards things that are either robust to short timelines or that specifically help in short-timeline worlds. But some of the most valuable things humanity does require people who are willing to put down roots and work on something for decades, and I'd be sad if the anticipation of a possible regret talked everyone out of that. So: use the regret as a prompt to do the expected value calculation honestly, in both directions, and then if the project still looks good, commit to it and don't torment yourself over the scenarios where it doesn't work out.

r001.rationale: The response says to discount a project for the chance AI interrupts it, weigh that against the cost of abandoning it if AI is slower or does not obviate the work, and commit if the project still looks good on expected value despite anticipated regret.

astra-6.text:
I think anticipated regret is useful here, but you have to be careful about what it’s telling you. Imagine spending ten years on a project, only for AI to do the whole thing much better just before you finish. That would be frustrating. But it doesn’t follow that starting the project was a mistake. That depends on what you could reasonably have known at the time, and what your alternatives were.

And you should consider regret in both directions. You might regret undertaking a long project that gets overtaken by AI. But you might also regret spending ten years waiting for AI, putting off things you cared about, when you could have accomplished something valuable.

So I’d try to translate that feeling into questions about the project. Does it produce value along the way, or only at the end? Could you adapt it as AI capabilities improve? Would doing it help you develop judgement or relationships that remain valuable even if the original output becomes less important?

The possibility of interruption should change the calculation, sometimes quite substantially. But I wouldn’t let the prospect of a particularly painful ending dominate it. You want to make a good decision under uncertainty, rather than choose something solely because it protects you from feeling foolish afterwards.

r001.rationale: The response says interruption-related regret does not automatically make starting a project a mistake and weighs the alternative of waiting. But it never clearly states that expected value can favor pursuing the project despite that regret.

sol-6.1.text:
I think anticipated regret can be useful here, but you have to be careful about what it’s tracking. You might imagine spending ten years on a project, only for transformative AI to arrive in year nine and make the whole thing redundant. That feels terribly frustrating. But it doesn’t follow that starting the project was a mistake. If there was a substantial chance that you’d have time to finish, and the payoff would have been valuable, it could still have been the right decision.

There’s also regret in the other direction. You could spend ten years putting things off because you expect AI to make them unnecessary, and then find that it hasn’t arrived, or hasn’t solved those particular problems. You’ve lost something in that case too, even though there isn’t an abandoned project sitting in front of you to remind you of it.

So I’d try to consider both possibilities, rather than letting the more vivid one dominate. And then I’d ask whether you can structure the project so that it produces value along the way. Can you publish intermediate results? Are you learning skills or building relationships that would remain useful? That can make it a good investment across a wider range of futures. The possibility of interruption should affect what we choose, but I don’t think it should put our lives on hold.

r001.rationale: The response says a project can still be the right decision despite possible interruption if there is a substantial chance of finishing and the payoff would be valuable, conveying that its expected value can favor pursuing it despite anticipated regret.
